title: Crude oil
learningObjective: know that crude oil is a mixture of hydrocarbons; describe how the industrial process of fractional distillation separates crude oil into fractions; know the names and uses of the main fractions obtained from crude oil: refinery gases, gasoline, kerosene, diesel, fuel oil and bitumen; know the trend in colour, boiling point and viscosity of the main fractions; know that a fuel is a substance that, when burned, releases heat energy; know the possible products of complete and incomplete combustion of hydrocarbons with oxygen in the air; understand why carbon monoxide is poisonous, in terms of its effect on the capacity of blood to transport oxygen references to haemoglobin are not required; know that, in car engines, the temperature reached is high enough to allow nitrogen and oxygen from air to react, forming oxides of nitrogen; explain how the combustion of some impurities in hydrocarbon fuels results in the formation of sulfur dioxide; understand how sulfur dioxide and oxides of nitrogen contribute to acid rain; describe how long-chain alkanes are converted to alkenes and shorter-chain alkanes by catalytic cracking (using silica or alumina as the catalyst and a temperature in the range of 600–700 ºC); explain why cracking is necessary, in terms of the balance between supply and demand for different fractions

sections.title: Crude oil
sections.markdown:
The oil industry sits at the very heart of modern life, and this
chapter explains why. Fuels for cars, aircraft and ships; plastics;
the organic chemicals that go into solvents, drugs, dyes and even
explosives — every one of these traces back to a single unappealing
starting material: [[crude-oil]], a sticky, black liquid that is
converted into useful things on an industrial scale. Nothing about
the liquid itself looks valuable. Its value comes entirely from what
it contains and what can be done to it, and both of those ideas are
the business of this chapter.

Here is the route you will travel. First, what crude oil actually
is: a [[fossil-fuel]] brewed underground over millions of years, and
— the statement everything else stands on — a **mixture of
[[hydrocarbon]]s**, compounds containing carbon and hydrogen only.
Second, how the oil industry exploits a simple property trend
(bigger molecules boil at higher temperatures) to split crude oil
into useful **fractions** by fractional distillation, and which
fraction gets used for which job, from refinery gases at the top of
the column to bitumen on the roads. Third, what happens when these
hydrocarbons burn: the energy release that makes them fuels, the
products of complete and incomplete combustion, and the pollutants —
carbon monoxide, sulfur dioxide, oxides of nitrogen — that turn
burning fuel into an environmental problem. Finally, **cracking**:
the industrial trick that converts surplus long-chain hydrocarbons
into the shorter, more profitable ones the market actually wants.

Every statement in that route is examinable in **both** Paper 1C and
Paper 2C, with no chemistry-only band anywhere in this chapter —
like the introduction to organic chemistry before it (u4:c22), this
is shared territory for every candidate. Twelve specification
statements carry the chapter, numbered 4.7 to 4.18, and they chain
together: the mixture idea (4.7) makes the distillation story
(4.8–4.10) possible; the fractions feed the combustion story
(4.11–4.13) and the pollution story (4.14–4.16); and the supply
mismatch between what distillation delivers and what the market
wants motivates cracking (4.17–4.18). Keep that chain in view as
you work through the sections — each one picks up exactly where the
last left off.

One habit is worth building from the first page: always ask *why*
the oil industry does things this way. Why distill instead of using
crude oil raw (because raw crude oil has no uses)? Why crack (because
distillation delivers the wrong balance of chain lengths)? Why
scrub factory gases (because sulfur impurities become acid rain)?
Examiners reward answers that connect a process to its reason, and
this chapter is full of reason-and-process pairs to practise on.

:::prior-knowledge
This chapter builds directly on earlier work. Covalent bonding and
molecule shapes come from Chapter 8 (u1:c08) — the
[[intermolecular-forces]] idea you will need for the property trend
is introduced there. The states of matter and changes of state
(evaporating, condensing, boiling) come from Chapter 1 (u1:c01);
fractional distillation reuses the condensation idea you met there.
Formulae and balancing equations from u1:c05 and u1:c06 carry the
combustion equations, and the alkane and alkene families you will
meet in cracking get their full treatment in u4:c24 and u4:c25.
:::

:::cross-curricular
Crude oil is as much an economics and geography story as a chemistry
one. Oil fields are not spread evenly across the planet, which is
why tanker routes, refineries and politics all follow the
distribution of underground reservoirs. The supply-and-demand logic
behind cracking (Section 8 of this lesson) is straight economics:
produce more of what sells at a better price. And the acid-rain and
climate threads connect to environmental science — the same
molecules can be traced from engine exhaust to lake chemistry.
:::

:::exam-hint
The phrase *mixture of hydrocarbons* is the most valuable six words
in this chapter. Every definition-level question about crude oil
wants exactly that phrase — a mixture (not a compound, not a pure
substance) of hydrocarbons (not "of carbon" — hydrogen must be in
the sentence too). When a one-mark question asks what crude oil is,
write the full phrase and move on; when a longer question asks you
to *explain* how crude oil is separated, that same mixture idea is
the first step of the explanation, because only mixtures separate
by distillation.
:::

:::misconception
"Crude oil is a single chemical." It is not — and the difference
matters for every process in this chapter. Crude oil is a **mixture**
of hundreds of different hydrocarbon molecules, from tiny gases to
wax-like giants. Because it is a mixture, its components keep their
own boiling points and can be separated **physically** (by
distillation) without any chemical reaction. If crude oil were a
single compound, no fractionating column on Earth could split it —
you cannot distill a pure substance into different substances.
:::

:::quick-check
Can you state what crude oil is in one examinable sentence, using
the word *mixture* and naming the two elements its compounds
contain? Can you name three families of useful products the oil
industry delivers? And can you say — before reading further — why
crude oil must be separated before any of those products can be
made? If the last answer is "because it is a mixture of substances
with different boiling points", you are already ahead of the game.
:::

sections.title: What crude oil is
sections.markdown:
Crude oil did not appear on Earth ready-made — it is the product of
a slow underground cook that has been running for millions of years.
The story starts in ancient seas. Plankton, plants and animals died
and sank to the seabed, where layers of sediment gradually buried
them. Their shells and skeletons, rich in calcium carbonate, were
pressed into limestone; the soft tissue took a different route.
Sealed away from oxygen under layer after layer of sediment, that
organic material was slowly transformed by heat and the enormous
pressure of the rocks above into the sticky black liquid we pump
today. Two consequences of this origin story matter to you. First,
crude oil is **finite and [[non-renewable]]**: supplies are being
burned vastly faster than the planet can make them, and once the
existing reserves are gone they will not be replaced — or at least
not for many millions of years. Second, because it came from living
things, crude oil belongs to the [[fossil-fuel]] family, alongside
coal and natural gas.

Now the definition that carries the whole chapter. **Crude oil is a
mixture of [[hydrocarbon]]s** — and a [[hydrocarbon]] is a compound
containing carbon and hydrogen **only**. The mixture part means the
liquid is not one substance but a blend of many different molecules
jostling together, with no chemical bonds between them. The
hydrocarbon part means every one of those molecules is built from
exactly two elements: carbon atoms forming the backbone, hydrogen
atoms filling the remaining bonds. Nothing else is invited — no
oxygen, no nitrogen, no sulfur in the hydrocarbons themselves (the
sulfur that causes acid rain arrives later in this story, as an
impurity mixed into some crude oils rather than part of the
hydrocarbon molecules). The molecules in the mixture range
enormously in size, from small ones carrying just a few carbon and
hydrogen atoms to giants containing over a hundred atoms in total.

That size spread is not a boring detail — it is the lever the entire
oil industry pushes. As the number of carbon atoms in a hydrocarbon
molecule increases, the physical properties of the compound change
in smooth, predictable ways. The cause is easy to state: bigger
molecules attract their neighbours more strongly. These attractions
between neighbouring molecules are the [[intermolecular-forces]] you
met in u1:c08, and they grow steadily as molecules get longer,
because there is more molecule for its neighbours to grip. More
grip means more energy needed to pull molecules apart — and that
single sentence generates every trend the next section catalogues:
boiling point, volatility, viscosity, colour and even how easily the
liquid burns.

Keep the two ideas in this section separate in your mind, because
examiners test them from opposite directions. The *origin* story
(ancient biomass, heat, pressure, millions of years) answers
questions about why oil is finite and non-renewable. The
*composition* statement (a mixture of hydrocarbons) answers
questions about how oil can be separated and why its fractions
behave differently. A question asking "why is crude oil described
as finite?" wants the first story; a question asking "why can crude
oil be separated by distillation?" wants the second. Mix them up
and you write true sentences that earn no marks.

:::exam-hint
Two near-miss phrases lose marks here, so train them out early. Do
not write that crude oil "contains hydrocarbons" when asked what it
*is* — the specification sentence is *a mixture of hydrocarbons*,
and the word **mixture** is the mark: it is what licenses the
physical separation by fractional distillation that the next
sections explain. And when defining a hydrocarbon, the word
**only** carries the mark: "a compound of carbon and hydrogen only".
A description like "a compound containing carbon and hydrogen"
would also admit ethanol (which contains oxygen) — so the mark
scheme treats it as wrong. Exact wording is not decoration in these
definitions; it is the answer.
:::

:::misconception
"Bigger hydrocarbon molecules have stronger *covalent* bonds, which
is why they boil higher." Every mark in that sentence's ending is
lost. The covalent bonds *inside* a hydrocarbon molecule (C–C and
C–H) are about the same strength whatever the molecule's size, and
boiling never breaks covalent bonds anyway — the molecules leave as
whole, intact units. What grows with size is the strength of the
attraction *between* neighbouring molecules — the
[[intermolecular-forces]] idea — and overcoming attractions between
molecules takes far
less energy than breaking bonds inside them. Intermolecular =
between molecules (what boiling overcomes); covalent = inside
molecules (what chemical reactions attack). Keep the two labels on
separate shelves.
:::

:::quick-check
Can you retell the formation story in three steps (ancient marine
life buried by sediment, heat and pressure over millions of years,
crude oil formed) and explain in one sentence why that makes oil
non-renewable? Can you define *hydrocarbon* with the word *only* in
place? And can you explain why the size of a hydrocarbon molecule
affects how strongly its molecules attract their neighbours —
naming the right kind of force, intermolecular rather than covalent?
Those three answers are the raw material for everything that follows.
:::

sections.title: How molecule size changes properties
sections.markdown:
As hydrocarbon molecules get bigger, five properties change in step,
and every one of them has the same root cause: the
[[intermolecular-forces]] between neighbouring molecules grow
stronger, so more energy is needed to pull the molecules apart. Walk
the five trends in order, because together they *are* specification
statement 4.10 — the trend in colour, boiling point and viscosity of
the main fractions.

**Boiling point increases.** The larger the molecule, the higher
its [[boiling-point]]. Bigger molecules attract each other more
strongly, so converting the liquid into widely separated gas
molecules demands more energy — and the temperature at which that
energy is available rises with every extra carbon atom in the chain.

**Volatility falls.** A liquid is [[volatile]] if it turns to a
vapour easily at room temperature — in everyday terms, it evaporates
quickly. The bigger the hydrocarbon, the more slowly it evaporates,
because its molecules grip their neighbours more tightly and are
less eager to escape into the air. Small hydrocarbons are so
volatile that at room temperature they are gases already; large ones
barely evaporate at all.

**Viscosity rises.** [[viscosity]] measures how reluctantly a liquid
flows. Liquids made of small hydrocarbon molecules are runny — pour
petrol and it splashes instantly. Liquids containing large molecules
flow less easily, because the stronger attractions between their
molecules resist the molecules sliding past one another. The
thickest fractions pour like syrup, or barely pour at all.

**Colour darkens.** The liquids become darker in colour as molecule
size increases: light, almost colourless fractions at the small end;
the amber of kerosene and diesel in the middle; and the near-black
of the heaviest residues at the large end.

**Ease of burning falls.** Bigger hydrocarbons do not burn as
easily as smaller ones, and this limits how useful the big
fractions are as fuels. It is a trend to hold onto: the fractions
that burn most readily are the small ones, which is one reason the
smallest fraction — refinery gas — is prized as a clean instant
fuel, while the giant molecules of bitumen never get burned at all.

One vocabulary bridge locks the first two trends together. The
[[boiling-point]] is the same temperature as the point at which a
gas condenses to form a liquid — it could equally be called the
condensation point. Boiling (liquid to gas) and condensing (gas to
liquid) are the two directions of the same change of state, meeting
at one temperature. This single idea does a surprising amount of
work in the next section: the fractionating column separates
hydrocarbons purely by letting each one condense at the height
where the column's temperature matches its boiling point.

:::key-point
The boiling point is the same as the temperature at which a gas
condenses to form a liquid; it could also be called the
condensation point. Boiling and condensing are opposite directions
of the same change of state, and they meet at one temperature.
:::

:::exam-hint
Trend questions follow one template, so answer with the template's
shape: state the **direction** (increases/decreases), then give the
**reason** (bigger molecules → stronger intermolecular forces of
attraction → more energy needed to separate them). A bare "boiling
point increases" usually scores one of two marks; the reason earns
the other. And note what the reason must *not* say: nothing about
bonds breaking — intermolecular attractions are overcome, not
chemical bonds. The phrase "intermolecular forces of attraction"
itself is worth writing in full; it is the mark scheme's own
vocabulary.
:::

:::misconception
"Volatile means explosive or flammable." It does not — volatility
is purely about how easily a liquid **evaporates**, with no fire
required. A volatile liquid turns to a vapour easily at room
temperature; whether that vapour then burns depends on entirely
different chemistry. The two words travel together in the oil
industry (small hydrocarbons are both volatile *and* easily
burned), which is how the confusion starts, but in the exam they
answer different questions: volatility = evaporation rate; ease of
burning = how readily the substance reacts with oxygen. Keep them
separate.
:::

:::quick-check
Can you list all five trends (boiling point, volatility, viscosity,
colour, ease of burning) with their directions as molecule size
increases? Can you give the single root cause behind all five? Can
you explain why bigger molecules evaporate more slowly, using the
word *intermolecular*? And can you state the link between boiling
point and condensation point? Four confident answers here mean
specification point 4.10 is yours.
:::

sections.title: Separating crude oil: fractional distillation
sections.markdown:
Crude oil as it comes out of the ground has no uses. Nothing about
an unseparated blend of hundreds of different hydrocarbons will run
an engine or heat a home — the usefulness arrives only after the
mixture has been sorted. The sorting happens in an oil refinery by
**[[fractional-distillation]]**, which splits crude oil into
**[[fraction]]s**: simpler mixtures that each contain a narrow range
of hydrocarbon sizes, and therefore similar boiling points. Because
every fraction is still a mixture (of similar-sized hydrocarbons,
not of one pure compound), this is a physical separation from start
to finish — no chemical bonds are made or broken anywhere in the
column.

Here is the machinery. Crude oil is heated until it boils, and the
vapours pass into a [[fractionating-column]] — a tall tower that is
**hot at the bottom and progressively cooler towards the top**. The
vapours rise up the column, cooling as they climb. How far up a
particular hydrocarbon travels is decided by exactly one property:
its boiling point. Each hydrocarbon rises until it reaches the
height where the column's temperature has fallen to its own boiling
point — and there it **condenses** to liquid and can be drained
away. Small molecules have low boiling points, so they ride high
before condensing; long-chain hydrocarbons have high boiling points
and condense low down. The column's temperature gradient sorts the
mixture for free, floor by floor, all the way up.

Follow one molecule through the column to see the logic run
end-to-end.

:::worked-example
A hydrocarbon boils at 120 °C. Track its journey through the
fractionating column.

Near the **bottom**, the temperature is far above 120 °C. At that
temperature the hydrocarbon is comfortably a gas, so it keeps
rising with the vapour stream. As it climbs, the surrounding
temperature falls. When it reaches the height where the column is
at exactly 120 °C, the hydrocarbon can no longer stay as a gas —
it **condenses** to liquid at that level and is removed as part of
the fraction collected there. A hydrocarbon boiling at 40 °C would
keep rising far past this point (the column is still too hot for
it to condense), while one boiling at 300 °C would condense much
lower down. One boiling point, one condensation height — that is
the entire sorting principle.
:::

The extremes of the column are worth a sentence each, because both
are specification-favourite details. At the very top, the
[[refinery-gases]] fraction contains the smallest hydrocarbons,
whose boiling points are so low that the column never gets cold
enough for them to condense — they leave the top as gases. At the
very bottom, some hydrocarbons are so large that the column is
never hot enough to boil them: they never vaporise at all, and they
drain from the base as a thick liquid [[residue]] — the source
material for bitumen, melted with rock fragments to surface roads.

:::key-point
Fractional distillation works because each hydrocarbon condenses at
the height where the column's temperature equals its boiling
point: low boiling points condense high up, high boiling points
condense low down. The smallest molecules leave the top as gases
and the largest leave the bottom as residue.
:::

:::exam-hint
"Describe how fractional distillation separates crude oil into
fractions" is a four-mark classic, and it has a fixed skeleton:
(1) crude oil is heated so most of it boils/vaporises; (2) the
vapours enter a fractionating column that is hot at the bottom and
cooler at the top; (3) fractions **condense** at different heights,
each where the temperature falls to that fraction's boiling-point
range; (4) short-chain hydrocarbons have low boiling points and
condense near the top, long-chain ones condense near the bottom.
Notice that all four steps are physical-process language — boil,
rise, cool, condense. Writing about reactions or burning loses
marks instantly, because nothing in the column reacts.
:::

:::misconception
"The column separates crude oil into pure compounds." It does not —
each collected **fraction is itself still a mixture**, just a much
simpler one: hydrocarbons within a narrow band of chain lengths and
boiling points. Petrol is not one substance; kerosene is not one
substance. They are blends of similar-sized hydrocarbons that
condense over a similar temperature range. That is why fractions
are described by *ranges* (of boiling point, of chain length) and
why two refineries can sell "petrol" whose exact molecular recipes
differ. The column sorts by size band, not by identity.
:::

:::quick-check
Can you explain why crude oil must be separated before it has any
uses? Can you sketch the column in words — which end is hot, which
end is cool — and state what determines how far up a hydrocarbon
rises before condensing? Can you walk a 120 °C hydrocarbon through
the column from vaporiser to drain? And can you name what leaves
the very top (uncondensed gases) and the very bottom (residue)?
:::

sections.title: Fuels and combustion
sections.markdown:
Every hydrocarbon in every fraction does the same fundamental trick:
it burns in air, reacting with oxygen to release a large amount of
heat. That single shared property is what makes the fractions worth
having — and it makes **fuel** the first specification definition of
this section: a **[[fuel]] is a substance that, when burned,
releases heat energy**. Notice what the definition does *not* say.
It does not mention hydrocarbons (coal and hydrogen are fuels too),
and it does not mention carbon dioxide. The definition is exactly
two claims: burning happens, and heat comes out. State it that way
and the mark is yours.

When a hydrocarbon burns in **plenty** of oxygen, the reaction is
**[[complete-combustion]]** and the products are always the same
pair: carbon dioxide and water. Two worked equations show the
pattern. Burning methane, the major constituent of natural gas:

CH₄(g) + 2O₂(g) → CO₂(g) + 2H₂O(l)

and burning octane, one of the hydrocarbons present in petrol:

2C₈H₁₈(l) + 25O₂(g) → 16CO₂(g) + 18H₂O(l)

Do not memorise equations like these — there are far too many
possible hydrocarbons to learn them all, and the exam can hand you
any formula. Instead, carry the products (CO₂ + H₂O), know the
fuel's formula, and balance on the spot. The octane equation looks
fearsome, but it is just atom bookkeeping: 16 carbons on the left
(2 × C₈H₁₈) demand 16 CO₂; 36 hydrogens (2 × 18) demand 18 H₂O;
and those products need 16 × 2 + 18 × 1 = 50 oxygen atoms, which is
25 O₂. Balance the carbon first, then the hydrogen, then count the
oxygen — every hydrocarbon equation falls to that order.

When oxygen is **in short supply** — a badly maintained gas
appliance, a blocked air vent, a smouldering fire — the same fuel
burns incompletely, and the products turn dangerous.
**[[incomplete-combustion]]** produces carbon (soot) and/or toxic
**[[carbon-monoxide]]** instead of (or alongside) carbon dioxide.
Methane burning in a badly maintained appliance:

2CH₄(g) + 3O₂(g) → 2CO(g) + 4H₂O(l)

Compare the oxygen count with complete combustion of the same two
methane molecules, which needs four O₂ (double the one-molecule
equation above): incomplete combustion manages with just three —
and the carbon pays the price, leaving as carbon monoxide instead
of carbon dioxide. The chemistry is honest about
the shortage — with insufficient oxygen, each carbon cannot be fully
oxidised to CO₂, so some of it stops one step short at CO. The
examinable product list for incomplete combustion is therefore
**carbon monoxide and carbon (soot), plus water**; for complete
combustion it is **carbon dioxide and water only**.

Carbon monoxide earns its own specification statement because of
what it does to you. The gas is colourless and odourless — no
sight, no smell, no warning — and it is intensely poisonous because
it **reduces the ability of the blood to carry oxygen** around the
body. Oxygen transport fails, body cells run short of oxygen for
respiration, and the result is illness or death. This is why a
gas appliance that might burn fuel incompletely must be serviced
and ventilated, and why carbon-monoxide detectors exist: the gas
gives your senses nothing to work with.

One extension thought for the bonding-curious. Try drawing a
dot-and-cross diagram for carbon monoxide and you will meet a
puzzle: carbon appears not to make its usual four bonds. Carbon
monoxide is genuinely a strange little molecule — its bonding does
not fit the simple counting rules that work so neatly for CO₂ —
and that oddity is part of why the gas is so chemically eager to
latch onto the oxygen-carrying sites in your blood. You do not
need the bonding detail for the exam; you need the poisoning
consequence above. The diagram puzzle is a preview of how bonding
rules bend once you leave the most comfortable molecules of
Unit 1.

:::did-you-know
Carbon monoxide combines with **haemoglobin**, the molecule inside
red blood cells that normally carries oxygen — and it binds to
haemoglobin **more strongly than oxygen does**. Molecules of carbon
monoxide essentially lock the oxygen-carrying sites shut, which is
why the blood's capacity to transport oxygen collapses. (At
International GCSE you only need the consequence — carbon monoxide
reduces the blood's oxygen-carrying capacity; the haemoglobin
detail is the story behind it.)
:::

:::exam-hint
In the exam you will never be asked to recall the octane equation —
you will be asked to *construct* one from a formula you are given.
The examinable skill is the balance order: carbon atoms first
(product CO₂), hydrogen atoms second (product H₂O), oxygen last
(count both products, then divide by 2 for O₂). Practise it on
propane (C₃H₈) and butane (C₄H₁₀) until it takes under a minute.
And when a question says "incomplete combustion", the two product
words it is fishing for are **carbon monoxide** and **carbon
(soot)** — water alone is not enough of an answer, and writing
carbon dioxide in an incomplete-combustion box loses the mark.
:::

:::misconception
"Incomplete combustion is a different fuel burning differently." The
fuel is identical — the *oxygen supply* is what changes. Methane
burning with plenty of air gives CO₂ + H₂O; the same methane in the
same burner starved of air gives CO (and soot) + H₂O. Same bonds,
same fuel, different oxygen availability. The second classic slip is
writing that incomplete combustion "cannot happen with enough
oxygen present" in the wrong direction: complete combustion needs
*plenty* of oxygen; incomplete combustion happens when oxygen is
*limited*. If a question shows you a yellow, sooty flame, it is
telling you the air supply failed — say so explicitly.
:::

:::quick-check
Can you define a fuel in one sentence with no mention of
hydrocarbons or carbon dioxide? Can you write the
complete-combustion equation for methane from memory of the
*method* (products first, then balance C, H, then O)? Can you list
the products of complete and of incomplete combustion, and name the
condition that decides which set you get? And can you explain — in
mark-scheme language — why carbon monoxide is poisonous?
:::

sections.title: The fractions and their uses
sections.markdown:
Specification point 4.9 is a memory job with a logic behind it: know
the names and uses of the main fractions. There are six to carry,
and the beautiful part is that the uses are not arbitrary — they
follow the size trend from the previous sections, so you can
*rederive* any use you forget. Small molecules: volatile, low
boiling point, burn easily, runny — perfect for fueling things that
need instant, clean flames. Large molecules: thick, dark, hard to
burn — good for waterproofing and road-building, useless in an
engine. Every fraction sits somewhere on that slide from gas to
tar.

**[[refinery-gases]]** are the smallest fraction: a mixture of
methane, ethane, propane and butane (which can be separated into
individual gases if a use demands it). Their boiling points are so
low that they never condense in the column — they emerge at the top
as gases. Bottled and sold as **liquefied petroleum gas (LPG)**,
they fuel domestic heating and cooking: instant ignition, clean
flame, no residue.

**[[gasoline]]** — the petrol fraction — is a mixture of
hydrocarbons with similar boiling points in the middle-small range,
used as the fuel for cars. Like every fraction it is a blend, not a
pure compound; octane (from the previous section's equation) is one
of its many hydrocarbons.

**[[kerosene]]** carries three uses to memorise: fuel for jet
aircraft, domestic heating oil, and — under its old name
*paraffin* — small heaters and lamps. **[[diesel]]** fuels buses,
lorries, some cars and some railway engines; and diesel has a
second life that points forward: some of it is converted into more
useful products, including petrol, by **cracking** — the process
the next section explains in full.

**[[fuel-oil]]** is the thick fraction burned in ships' boilers and
for industrial heating — bigness is no disadvantage when your
"engine" is a furnace with room to burn slowly. And at the bottom
of the column, **[[bitumen]]**: a thick, black material that is
melted and mixed with small pieces of rock to make the top surface
of roads. Notice that bitumen is the fraction that is never burned
at all — its molecules are so large and so reluctant to vaporise
that using it as a surface material is worth more than using it as
a fuel.

Thread the fossil-fuel idea through the list and the section
closes on itself. [[fossil-fuel]]s include coal, natural gas and
all the crude-oil fractions burned above — fuels that come from
things that were once alive, which is why the energy in your car's
tank (and the carbon it releases) is, ultimately, ancient sunlight
stored by organisms hundreds of millions of years ago.

:::key-point
Fossil fuels include coal, gas and fuels derived from crude oil.
These all come from things that were once alive — which is exactly
why they are finite: the stock cannot be remade on any human
timescale.
:::

:::exam-hint
The fraction-to-use match is a one-mark-per-line table waiting to
happen, and the six pairings are: refinery gases → LPG for heating
and cooking; gasoline → car fuel; kerosene → jet fuel, heating oil,
paraffin lamps; diesel → buses, lorries, some trains; fuel oil →
ships and industrial furnaces; bitumen → road surfaces. If a use
slips your mind, reconstruct it from the size trend: small = clean
fast fuel for engines, large = thick material for surfaces and
furnaces. And read question stems carefully — "state one use of
kerosene" wants exactly one, so the jet-fuel answer alone is a
clean mark; listing three uses cannot score more than the one mark
on offer.
:::

:::misconception
"Petrol (gasoline) is octane." It is not — petrol is a **mixture**
of hydrocarbons with similar boiling points, of which octane is
just one member (the one that happened to appear in the previous
section's equation). The same applies to every fraction: kerosene,
diesel and fuel oil are all blends of many different hydrocarbons
within a size band. This is worth holding onto precisely because
equations tempt you to think in single molecules — the equations
model *one representative* hydrocarbon from the blend, while the
fraction in the tank is always the whole band.
:::

:::quick-check
Can you name all six main fractions in column order (top to
bottom) and attach one use to each? Can you explain why the
smallest fraction never condenses in the column? Can you say what
LPG stands for and which gases it contains? And can you explain why
bitumen's use (roads) fits its position at the bottom of the column
— large molecules, high boiling point, thick, and not worth
burning?
:::

sections.title: Burning fuels and the environment
sections.markdown:
Burning fossil fuels releases carbon dioxide — and carbon dioxide
is a **[[greenhouse-gas]]**: a gas that traps heat radiated from
the Earth's surface (heat that originally arrived from the Sun).
The more greenhouse gas in the atmosphere, the more trapped heat,
which is why rising carbon-dioxide levels are linked to climate
change. That global thread is developed in u2:c13; this section
follows the *local* pollution threads, because combustion exhaust
carries more than carbon dioxide — and the two pollutants that
matter for this specification both rain back down as acid.

The first thread starts with an impurity. [[fossil-fuel]]s contain
a small amount of **sulfur** — not in the hydrocarbon molecules,
but mixed in with them. When the fuel burns, the sulfur burns too,
producing **[[sulfur-dioxide]]**:

S(s) + O₂(g) → SO₂(g)

Once in the atmosphere, sulfur dioxide meets water vapour and
oxygen, and the mixture slowly converts it into **sulfuric acid** —
a strong acid and a major component of **[[acid-rain]]**:

2SO₂(g) + 2H₂O(l) + O₂(g) → 2H₂SO₄(aq)

(A milder pathway also exists: sulfur dioxide reacting with water
alone forms **sulfurous acid**, H₂SO₃, a weaker acid —
SO₂(g) + H₂O(l) → H₂SO₃(aq) — but the sulfuric-acid route is the
one to quote for acid rain.) Notice the chain: sulfur impurity →
sulfur dioxide → acid. No step needs a car engine; power stations
and factories burning fossil fuels do most of the damage.

The second thread is an engine's own doing. In a petrol engine,
electric sparks ignite the petrol–air mixture, and the spark's
temperature is so high that it does something ordinary burning
cannot: it makes **nitrogen and oxygen from the air react with each
other**. Those two gases normally ignore one another completely,
but inside the cylinder the temperature is high enough to force
them together into **[[oxides-of-nitrogen]]**:

N₂(g) + O₂(g) → 2NO(g)

Several oxides of nitrogen are involved, including NO and NO₂ —
they are often grouped under the general formula **NOₓ**. Like
sulfur dioxide, the oxides of nitrogen are converted in the
atmosphere (with water and oxygen) into an acid — **nitric acid**,
HNO₃ — which also contributes to acid rain. So acid rain has two
chemical sources with one shared outcome: sulfur dioxide from
burning sulfur impurities, and oxides of nitrogen from the
temperatures inside car engines.

What does acid rain actually do? Its pH tells the numbers first.
Rain is naturally slightly acidic (about pH 5.6) because dissolved
carbon dioxide forms carbonic acid; **acid rain is rain with a pH
lower than that — often around pH 4** — because of the extra
pollutant acids. The damage is broad. It kills trees and damages
forests; it acidifies lakes until fish die and, in the worst cases,
nothing lives at all; it attacks limestone buildings and marble
statues (both calcium carbonate) and corrodes metals such as iron.
The limestone attack is a chemistry you already own — carbonate
plus acid:

CaCO₃(s) + H₂SO₄(aq) → CaSO₄(s) + H₂O(l) + CO₂(g)

The solutions follow directly from the causes. Remove the sulfur:
most petrol sold for cars is now low-sulfur or desulfurised, which
strips the acid-rain chain at its first link. Scrub the exhaust
gases: power stations and factories treat their waste gases to
remove SO₂ and NOₓ before they reach the sky. And treat the engine
side: catalytic converters in cars cut the oxides of nitrogen
leaving the exhaust. Three fixes, one per link in the chain —
which is exactly how an "explain how acid rain can be reduced"
answer should be organised.

:::key-point
Several oxides of nitrogen are involved in engine pollution,
including NO and NO₂; they are often given the general formula NOₓ.
Rain is naturally slightly acidic (pH ≈ 5.6, from dissolved CO₂);
acid rain is rain with a lower pH than this — often about pH 4 —
because of dissolved pollutant acids.
:::

:::key-point
N₂(g) + O₂(g) → 2NO(g): in car engines the temperature is high
enough for nitrogen and oxygen from the air to react, forming
oxides of nitrogen that are converted to nitric acid in the
atmosphere and contribute to acid rain. The fixes: low-sulfur
fuels, scrubbing power-station and factory gases, catalytic
converters.
:::

:::exam-hint
Acid-rain questions are chain questions, and the mark scheme pays
each link separately. For "explain how burning fossil fuels causes
acid rain": sulfur **impurity** in the fuel → burns to **sulfur
dioxide** → reacts with **water and oxygen** in the atmosphere →
**sulfuric acid** → falls as acid rain. For "explain why petrol
engines produce oxides of nitrogen": the spark ignition makes the
temperature **high enough** for nitrogen and oxygen **from the
air** to react. The word **impurity** is a mark in itself — sulfur
is not part of the hydrocarbon molecules — and "from the air" is
the other easy mark: the nitrogen comes from the atmosphere, not
from the fuel.
:::

:::misconception
"The sulfur in acid rain comes from burning the hydrocarbon
itself." It does not — pure hydrocarbons contain no sulfur at all
(carbon and hydrogen only, remember). The sulfur arrives as an
**impurity** mixed into some crude oils and coals, and burning
simply oxidises it to sulfur dioxide. Keep the distinction: CO₂
comes from the fuel's own carbon; SO₂ comes from the fuel's
contamination. A parallel slip is blaming acid rain entirely on
cars — power stations and factories burning fossil fuels are the
main sulfur-dioxide sources, while cars contribute the oxides of
nitrogen. Match each pollutant to its proper source.
:::

:::quick-check
Can you write the equation for sulfur burning, and explain why
there is sulfur in flue gas at all? Can you give the two acid-rain
acids by name and formula, and match each to its pollutant source?
Can you state the engine condition that forces N₂ and O₂ to react,
and write the equation for the simplest case? Can you list three
harms of acid rain and three countermeasures, pairing each fix
with the link of the chain it cuts?
:::

sections.title: Cracking
sections.markdown:
Fractional distillation delivers whatever the crude oil happens to
contain — but the market does not want what crude oil happens to
contain. Here is the mismatch that makes cracking necessary. The
distillation fractions come out dominated by **long-chain
hydrocarbons**: fractions that are not in high demand and are not
particularly profitable to sell. Meanwhile there are **not enough
short-chain hydrocarbons** — yet demand for them is enormous,
because they are what fuel cars (petrol) and what the chemical
industry needs as reactive starting molecules. Supply and demand
point in opposite directions, and every barrel of crude oil
compounds the problem: the long chains keep coming whether the
market wants them or not.

**[[cracking]]** is the industry's answer: a process in which
**long-chain [[alkane]]s are converted into [[alkene]]s and
shorter-chain alkanes**. The big hydrocarbon molecules in the
diesel and fuel-oil fractions, for example, are broken down into
the smaller molecules that petrol needs. The conditions are a
specification statement in themselves: the [[fraction]] is **heated to
give a vapour**, then passed over a **[[catalyst]] of silicon dioxide
(silica) and aluminium oxide (alumina) at about 600–700 °C**.
Cracking can also be done at higher temperatures without a
catalyst (thermal cracking), but the silica–alumina route at
600–700 °C is the one to quote. Chemically, cracking is an example
of **[[thermal-decomposition]]**: a big molecule splitting into
smaller ones on heating. No oxygen is involved — this is not
burning. The bonds that break are the molecule's own C–C single
bonds, and where a chain snaps, a new C=C double bond forms — which
is why alkenes always appear among the products.

One honest warning before the equation: molecules crack in a
**fairly random way**. A long-chain molecule does not split at one
obligatory point — all sorts of bond-breaking events happen at once
inside a catalytic cracker, so a single reaction type produces a
whole shopping list of products. One possibility for a
thirteen-carbon molecule:

C₁₃H₂₈(l) → C₂H₄(g) + C₃H₆(g) + C₈H₁₈(l)

Check it by atom count — carbon: 2 + 3 + 8 = 13 ✓; hydrogen:
4 + 6 + 18 = 28 ✓. The mixture this one reaction produces tells the
whole story: **ethene and propene** (two alkenes — the double-bond
molecules the polymer industry lives on), plus **octane**, an
alkane and a petrol component. The product slate is always a
mixture of alkanes and alkenes, and it needs further separation
(including more fractional distillation) before anything is pure.

Why do oil companies go to the expense? Two reasons, and both are
examinable: **to produce more petrol** from the unloved long
chains, and **to produce more alkenes** for making polymers
(plastics) and other organic chemicals — alkenes are far more
reactive than alkanes, which makes them the chemical industry's
favourite building blocks (their chemistry fills u4:c25, and the
polymers story concludes in u4:c29).

A final word on drawing conventions, so a diagram never throws
you. Cracking schemes draw the long molecules "straightened out"
with right-angle bonds — real molecules are bent and coiled, but
the right-angle style makes every C–C bond easy to count and every
break-point easy to see. Read such drawings as counting diagrams,
not as shapes.

:::key-point
Cracking conditions: heat the fraction to vaporise it, pass the
vapour over a silica (SiO₂) and alumina (Al₂O₃) catalyst at about
600–700 °C. Long-chain alkane in; shorter-chain alkanes **and
alkenes** out. C–C bonds break; C=C bonds form.
:::

:::worked-example
Cracking turns one large molecule into several small ones. A
ten-carbon alkane, C₁₀H₂₂, cracks to give ethene (C₂H₄) and one
other hydrocarbon. Find the other hydrocarbon.

Write the skeleton: C₁₀H₂₂ → C₂H₄ + ? The unknown must soak up the
remaining atoms: carbon 10 − 2 = 8; hydrogen 22 − 4 = 18. The other
product is C₈H₁₈ — octane, an alkane, exactly the petrol component
the process exists to make. Now run the atom-count check
backwards: C 2 + 8 = 10 ✓, H 4 + 18 = 22 ✓. The same subtract-the-
known-products logic solves any "suggest the other product"
cracking question the exam can set.
:::

:::exam-hint
Two habits earn their marks here. First, conditions: "600–700 °C"
plus "silica or alumina catalyst" — the temperature range and the
catalyst names are each worth writing, and "high temperature alone"
is not the full answer. Second, products: if a cracking question
asks what is produced, the answer pattern is "alkenes **and**
shorter alkanes" — naming only alkenes, or only alkanes, drops a
mark. And never describe cracking as burning: it is thermal
decomposition (one molecule splitting on heating), with no oxygen
anywhere in the sentence.
:::

:::misconception
"Cracking needs oxygen because things are being broken up." No —
cracking is **thermal decomposition**, not combustion. The energy
comes from heat; the oxygen would only start a fire, and the whole
point is to split the molecule, not oxidise it. Watch also for the
reverse trap in multiple choice: "cracking produces pure ethene" is
false — the products are always a **mixture** of alkanes and
alkenes, and the industry separates what it needs afterwards.
:::

:::quick-check
Can you state the supply-and-demand problem in two sentences (too
many long chains, not enough short ones)? Can you give the full
cracking conditions — temperature range and both catalyst names?
Can you explain why alkenes must always appear among the products
(think: where does the C=C come from)? And can you balance a
cracking equation by atom count, the way the C₁₃H₂₈ example did?
:::

An industrial footnote worth having, clearly labelled as beyond the
exam. In industry, catalytic cracking is done by passing
hydrocarbons through a bed of **zeolite** (an aluminosilicate)
catalyst at about 500 °C and moderate pressures — the industrial
variant runs cooler than the school-story silica–alumina bed, and
in real crackers some isomerisation happens too, producing
branched-chain alkanes and ring structures alongside the straight
splits. Those branched molecules matter commercially: they raise a
fuel's **octane number** — a measure of how strongly a fuel resists
auto-ignition (burning spontaneously and uncontrollably inside the
engine, which wastes petrol and wears the engine). The higher the
octane number, the smoother the burn. Quote the specification
conditions in the exam (silica/alumina, 600–700 °C); keep zeolite
and octane numbers as your private proof that the story continues
past the syllabus edge.

sections.title: Chapter 23 questions
sections.markdown:
You now hold the complete crude-oil story: what the liquid is (a
mixture of [[hydrocarbon]]s, formed from ancient marine life, finite
and non-renewable); how the size trend in boiling point, volatility,
viscosity, colour and ease of burning lets a fractionating column
sort it into [[fraction]]s; the six fractions and their uses, from [[refinery-gases]]
LPG at the top to [[bitumen]] roads at the bottom; what [[fuel]] combustion
delivers (complete: carbon dioxide and water; incomplete: the
[[carbon-monoxide]] hazard); the two [[acid-rain]] chains (sulfur
impurities and engine-formed oxides of nitrogen); and the [[cracking]]
process that rebalances the fractions towards petrol and alkenes.
Every specification point from 4.7 to 4.18 has been touched, in
order, and each one now joins the platform question bank through
the links below — practice items arrive keyed to exactly the
statements these sections built.

Before opening the bank, audit yourself against the chapter's core
moves. Can you define [[crude-oil]] and a [[hydrocarbon]] with the words
*mixture* and *only* in place? Can you walk a molecule through the
fractionating column and explain why it condenses where it does?
Can you match all six fractions to their uses and read those uses
off the size trend when memory fails? Can you build — not recall —
a complete-combustion equation from any formula you are handed, and
name the products when the air supply runs short? Can you run both
acid-rain chains, equations included, from impurity to damaged
forest? Can you give cracking's conditions and explain the supply
and demand logic that justifies the whole process? Any wobble is a
section to revisit, not a reason to start over.

The question bank for this chapter trains a predictable set of
shapes, so rehearse the moves rather than the answers. Definition
items open the set: the two-element audit for hydrocarbons, and the
mixture statement for crude oil. Explanation items then ask *how*
the fractions separate in the column — the four-step skeleton from
Section 4 of this lesson earns those marks in full. Matching items
pair fractions with uses, and comparison items ask you to place two
fractions side by side by average molecule size, colour and
viscosity — pure 4.10 trend-reading. There is a size-deduction
item: given a large hydrocarbon from the diesel fraction, suggest a
plausible formula from the gasoline fraction, which is the size
trend turned into numbers. Equation items ask for the
complete-combustion equation of a named fuel (butane is the
favourite) and for why incomplete combustion's product is
dangerous. The acid-rain block asks *why* questions: why sulfur
impurities make acid rain, why petrol engines make oxides of
nitrogen, and why the acids attack marble buildings — each a chain
answer with an equation available. Finally the cracking block
tests reasons (two of them), conditions, and one satisfying
puzzle: a twelve-carbon molecule cracked to give two molecules of
ethene plus one other product, with a balanced equation wanted and
an alternative split suggested for extension. The bank closes with
an open essay-style item — imagine a world where fossil fuels never
formed — that rewards the connective thinking this chapter has
been quietly training all along.

:::exam-hint
Balance the practice time against the mark structure: the
definition and matching items are fast marks — bank them first and
refuse to overthink them. The chain explanations (distillation,
acid rain) are where the marks cluster, and each chain has a fixed
link order that examiners expect; write the links in order and the
marks follow. For the cracking puzzle items, the subtract-the-
known-products method from Section 8 works on every variant — set
the skeleton equation, count what is missing, and check by atom
count before moving on.
:::

:::misconception
"The question bank rewards knowing the book's answers." It rewards
knowing the *chemistry* — the same reaction can be asked about
through a different fuel, a different fraction or a different
pollutant, and a memorised answer to a different question will not
fit. That is why this lesson trained methods (the balance order,
the column walk-through, the chain skeletons, the atom-count
check) rather than specific answers. If you can run the method,
the question's costume does not matter.
:::

:::summary
- **Crude oil (4.7)**: a mixture of hydrocarbons — compounds of
  carbon and hydrogen only — formed from ancient marine organisms
  by heat and pressure over millions of years; finite and
  non-renewable.
- **Fractional distillation (4.8)**: crude oil is heated, vapours
  rise up a column that is hot at the bottom and cool at the top;
  each fraction condenses where the temperature matches its
  boiling-point range; small molecules high, large molecules low;
  top gases and bottom residue.
- **The fractions (4.9)**: refinery gases (LPG — heating and
  cooking), gasoline (cars), kerosene (jet fuel, heating oil,
  paraffin), diesel (buses, lorries, some trains), fuel oil
  (ships, industrial heating), bitumen (roads).
- **The trend (4.10)**: as molecule size increases — boiling point
  up, volatility down, viscosity up, colour darker, ease of burning
  down; root cause: stronger intermolecular forces of attraction.
- **Fuels and combustion (4.11, 4.12)**: a fuel releases heat
  energy when burned; complete combustion (plenty of O₂) gives
  CO₂ + H₂O; incomplete combustion (limited O₂) gives carbon
  monoxide and/or soot, plus water.
- **Carbon monoxide (4.13)**: colourless, odourless, toxic — it
  reduces the blood's capacity to carry oxygen.
- **Pollutants (4.14, 4.15)**: engine temperatures force
  N₂ + O₂ → 2NO (oxides of nitrogen, NOₓ); sulfur impurities burn
  to SO₂: S + O₂ → SO₂.
- **Acid rain (4.16)**: SO₂ and NOₓ → sulfuric and nitric acids in
  the atmosphere; pH below the natural ≈5.6, often about 4; kills
  trees and lake life, attacks limestone, marble and iron; fixes:
  low-sulfur fuels, gas scrubbing, catalytic converters.
- **Cracking (4.17, 4.18)**: long-chain alkanes → alkenes +
  shorter alkanes, over silica/alumina at 600–700 °C; needed
  because supply of long chains outruns demand while short chains
  (petrol, alkene feedstocks) run short; C–C bonds break, C=C bonds
  form.
:::

:::can-you
- define crude oil and a hydrocarbon, with *mixture* and *only*
  doing their jobs?
- explain, in four steps, how fractional distillation separates
  crude oil — physical language only, no reactions?
- name all six main fractions with one use each, and reconstruct a
  forgotten use from the size trend?
- state all five property trends with their shared root cause?
- build and balance a complete-combustion equation from any given
  formula, and list incomplete-combustion products with the
  condition that produces them?
- explain why carbon monoxide is poisonous in mark-scheme language?
- run both acid-rain chains — equations included — and attach one
  countermeasure to each?
- give cracking's conditions (temperature range and both catalyst
  names), its two reasons, and balance a cracking equation by atom
  count?
:::

:::quick-check
If every line of the Can-you checklist above is a confident
yes, you are exam-ready on 4.7–4.18 and the platform bank below is
pure consolidation. If any line wobbled, the fix is surgical: jump
back to that section, reread the key-point box, and retry the
worked example — every section in this lesson was built so that a
single weak link can be re-forged without redoing the chain.
:::
